sense: doing or getting what one aimed at

terms.grammar: verb, third conjugation, intransitive; what is attempted is the subject, the person in the dative
evidence: Ter. And. 670: hāc nōn successit, aliā aggrediēmur viā
Caes. BG 7.26.1: quod rēs nūlla successerat
terms.comment: Rēs mihi succēdit, it is going well for me; sī ex sententiā successerit, if it turns out as we wish (Cic. Q. fr. 2.14.1, Lewis & Short). In Plautus and Terence the compound has only this sense (de Vaan 103, s.v. cēdō).

terms.grammar: phrase: gerō with rem and an adverb (bene, prosperē, fēlīciter)
evidence: Plaut. Mil. 936: bene ambulā, bene rem gerās
Traupman 188, 387: success, rēs fēlīciter gesta, rēs bene gesta
M-O s.v. succeed: rem prosperē (fēlīciter) gessī
terms.comment: Of someone who brings off what he set about, in business or in war. For how well someone does, see performance.
Lewis & Short: “a happy issue, good result, success (the usual signif.; perh. not ante-Aug.)”: Virgil, Livy, Ovid, Phaedrus, Quintilian, Tacitus; not Cicero’s word.
Literally “the thing not done”; also īnfectīs rēbus (Sallust, Nepos).

phrases.latin: Dēceptus sum, at nōn dēfatīgātus. … Hāc nōn successit, aliā aggrediēmur viā.
phrases.english: I’ve been foiled, but I’m not worn out. … That way didn’t work; we’ll go at it another way.
Safe journey, and success to you.
the success of the wicked draws more people in

successus.html: Lewis & Short leaves the vowel unmarked, as in suc-cēdo, cessi, cessum. After a long vowel ss was reduced to s in Augustan spelling (Quint. 1.7.20 records Cicero’s and Virgil’s caussae, cassus, divissiones), but cessī, cessum and successus kept ss, so the vowel before it is short.
